To castrate means to surgically remove the reproductive glands — most commonly the testicles (in a male). Since the testicles are the primary source of the hormone testosterone and the producer of sperm, removing them has major effects on the body, behavior, and reproductive ability of the person or animal.

In simpler terms: if you castrate a male, you take out his testicles.

Technically, the word can also apply to females, where it would mean removing the ovaries — but this usage is uncommon. For females, people usually say "spay" (in animals) or use medical terms like "oophorectomy" (in humans). When you hear "castrate" without any qualifier, almost always assume it means a male.

The word applies to both humans and animals.

In animals, castration is extremely common in farming and animal care:

  • A castrated bull is called a steer.
  • A castrated horse is called a gelding.
  • A castrated pig is called a barrow.
  • A castrated cat or dog (male) is commonly said to be neutered.

Farmers castrate male livestock to make them calmer and easier to manage, prevent unwanted breeding, and improve the quality of their meat.

In humans, castration has occurred in several contexts throughout history and medicine (more on that below).

1. Surgical castration — The testicles are physically removed through an operation. This is permanent and irreversible.

2. Chemical castration — No surgery is involved. Instead, drugs are used to drastically reduce the body's production of testosterone, effectively mimicking the hormonal result of surgical castration. Crucially, this is reversible — once the drugs are stopped, hormone levels can return to normal. The word "castrate" is still used here because the functional outcome (dramatic suppression of reproductive hormones) is the same, even though nothing is physically removed.

The reasons vary widely by context:

Medical reasons (humans):

  • Treating prostate cancer — prostate cancer feeds on testosterone, so removing that supply (via castration) slows or stops tumor growth.
  • Treating testicular cancer — the affected testicle is removed.
  • Managing certain hormonal conditions.

Animal husbandry:

  • To prevent unplanned breeding between animals.
  • To make male animals more docile, since testosterone drives aggression and dominance behavior.
  • To improve the flavor and texture of meat in livestock.

Historical and cultural reasons:

  • In parts of ancient and medieval history, men were castrated to serve as eunuchs — trusted servants, guardians of royal courts, or harem attendants — because their lack of testosterone was believed to make them less threatening or power-hungry.
  • In Renaissance Europe, young boys with exceptional singing voices were sometimes castrated to preserve their high-pitched voices into adulthood. These singers were called castrati (the plural of castrato). Castration before puberty prevents the voice from "breaking" (deepening) because testosterone drives that change.
  • Historically, castration was also used as a form of punishment or conquest in some cultures — a brutal act intended to humiliate and strip a man of his identity and virility.

Legal/criminal justice (modern, rare):

  • Some jurisdictions use chemical castration as a sentence or condition of parole for certain serious sexual offenders, as it dramatically reduces sexual drive.
What Are the Effects of Castration?

Because testosterone governs many aspects of male biology, removing its source has wide-ranging effects:

  • Loss of fertility — the person or animal can no longer reproduce.
  • Reduced or eliminated sex drive (libido).
  • Physical changes over time — reduced muscle mass, increased body fat, softer skin, potential bone density loss.
  • Behavioral changes — reduced aggression, reduced dominance behavior.
  • In prepubescent males — if castration happens before puberty, puberty either doesn't occur or is greatly diminished. This means the voice doesn't deepen, body hair doesn't develop normally, and the body retains more "feminine" proportions (wider hips, narrower shoulders).

With chemical castration, most of these effects reverse once treatment stops.

"Castrate" is also used metaphorically to mean: to strip something of its power, force, effectiveness, or essential quality — to render it weak and harmless.

For example:

  • "The final edit castrated the documentary — they removed every controversial scene."
  • "The amendment effectively castrated the bill, leaving it with no real enforcement power."

Here, nothing physical is happening. The word is being used to convey that something has been gutted of its strength or impact, the way a castrated male loses the driving force of testosterone.

This figurative use carries a deliberately strong, even harsh tone. A writer who says a law was "castrated" is expressing that it was not just weakened but fundamentally disempowered — made impotent (which is itself a related metaphor).

TermWhat it means
NeuterA broader, less clinical term — often used for animals (male or female); sometimes used as a polite substitute for "castrate."
SpaySpecifically for removing ovaries/reproductive organs in female animals.
GeldSpecifically means to castrate a horse.
EmasculateLiterally means to castrate, but today almost always used figuratively — to strip a man (or thing) of strength, dignity, or effectiveness.
EunuchA noun — a man who has been castrated (historically a person, not an action).
OrchiectomyThe medical/surgical term for the operation of removing a testicle.

• "The vet castrated the young bull before it was sold to the farm."
  • "Chemical castration was ordered by the court as a condition of his release."
  • "The editors castrated the novel — by the time they were done, its sharp political edges had been completely smoothed away."
  • "Historically, eunuchs were men who had been castrated, often in childhood, to serve in royal courts."

To castrate is to remove the testicles (or, rarely, ovaries) — permanently eliminating reproductive function and drastically reducing sex hormones — and, by extension, to figuratively strip anything of its essential power or force.
